column2: In a letter to Creeley dated October 7, 1955, a month after Rumaker's graduation, Duncan judges his three critical essays above the average for final-year work: informal papers, but showing a real critical intelligence, rare among graduates. Three critical pieces submitted to Duncan; comparison with the “graduate” level Consequences: Rumaker's work validated

At the college's worst moment (heat cut off, no salaries, tough chickens), the Fiores go from door to door in the snow, singing Christmas carols at the back doors Atmosphere: Cold, snow, affectionate gratitude Stakes: Dignity and generosity at the institution's lowest point

While finishing his military service at an army base in Newport News, Borregaard writes to the college to apply for admission; his application is dated January 8, 1956. application letter preserved in the Western Regional Archives Consequences: he will be the last student recruited
As the end of Albers's term approaches, Keller writes to President Griswold in an attempt to restore much of the pre-1950 program Consequences: Tensions over Albers's educational legacy

Elaine discovers the baby and the register in which Joan Ward appears as “Joan de Kooning”; she puts a happy face on a devastating event, having just undergone a hysterectomy. Words: “How wonderful. Bill and I always wanted a baby.” Atmosphere: Shock masked by gaiety; an intimate wound. Stakes: A turning point for Elaine and Bill as a couple.

Easter Monday was finished, the paint still wet, in time for the solo exhibition opening on April 2, the day after Easter Sunday that year; the work takes its name from the actual or anticipated day of its completion. opening on April 2, the day after Easter Consequences: the title closes a cycle opened eight years earlier by Black Friday
Letter from Sawyer to Osborn confirming that Albers's color course was a prerequisite for Gene Nalle's training

Elaine sketches the Yankees player Norm Siebern, a month after his major-league debut (Baseball #30-A–Siebern), in profile, curiously miniaturizing his six-foot-two frame, perhaps to evoke the distant view from the stands. Baseball #30-A–Siebern; a 1.88 m player

The play Medea, written by Duncan in the course of rehearsals, is performed twice, on August 29 and 30, 1956, in the very last days of the college. Consequences: The cast will leave with Duncan for San Francisco to keep working on the play with a view to a production.

Before hitchhiking to San Francisco, Rumaker writes that he had at first found Olson's work chaotic and gratuitous, but that a correction of his ear has made him hear the limpidity, the rhythm, the form — the limpidity Olson had demanded of him one evening by the dish rack. Quotation: “I now fully understand the meaning of limpidity”
Letter of application to the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation, cited for two phrases concerning her.

During a trip, the Alberses discover a backstrap loom in the village of Santo Tomás, described as an interesting variety of the usual type. On the same trip they meet Thornton Wilder. telar de cintura (backstrap loom); meeting with Thornton Wilder

“Lofty Shrine; Dallas Congregation Dedicates Synagogue,” Life, February 25, 1957, p. 62 — probably connected with Anni Albers's textiles for architecture (a hypothesis linked to her 1957 article “The Pliable Plane”). Life, XLII, February 25, 1957

The Artists Union is founded to demand government aid for artists; it becomes a popular social center for New York artists in the depths of the Depression Two years later, it will lobby the Federal Art Project (WPA) for wages and favorable conditions Consequences: Elaine and Milton Resnick meet there at a political action meeting, representing their art schools

With the rise of Nazism making their lives as artists impossible in Germany, the Alberses emigrate; Josef is invited to organize the art department of a new experimental rural college in North Carolina, Black Mountain College. They left paintings and photographs in Germany, brought over by the Fleischmanns in 1937 Consequences: For them, Black Mountain represents freedom; Anni describes the college as a void to be filled with creation

The Alberses emigrate to the United States in 1933, bringing with them the methodological baggage of the Bauhaus; there they find the serenity their work requires and can at last travel to the American cultures they knew only through books and museums. earlier references: publications by Max Schmidt, German archaeological collections (Max Uhle's excavations) Consequences: Anni Albers incorporates the Bauhaus methodology into her teaching at Black Mountain College.

The Nazis in power on January 30; growing harassment; closure announced by Mies to the students on August 10; at the same time Black Mountain College is taking shape; Philip Johnson and Edward M. M. Warburg (MoMA, who had visited the Bauhaus in 1927) propose inviting Josef to head the art department; the Alberses emigrate and arrive in New York on the S.S. Europa on November 24. Consequences: The Black Mountain adventure begins.

Philip Johnson and Edward M. M. Warburg, who had visited the Bauhaus in 1927, propose from MoMA that Josef be invited to head the art department of the new experimental, progressive school in North Carolina. Consequences: The Alberses emigrate to the United States

With the rise of Nazism making their lives as artists impossible in Germany, they emigrate to the United States: Josef is invited to create an art department in a new experimental college, Black Mountain College, in rural North Carolina. Consequences: Anni will describe Black Mountain as a void: a receptive space without preconceptions or program, to be filled with inventive creation; the college represented freedom for them

In emigrating in 1933, the Alberses bring with them the methodological baggage of the Bauhaus; they find there the peace to devote themselves to their work and discover at first hand cultures they had known only through books (Max Schmidt) or German museums (the collections of Max Uhle). books by Max Schmidt, collections brought back by Max Uhle Consequences: a prelude to their Latin American travels

The Nazi seizure of power on January 30; growing harassment; closure announced to the students by Mies on August 10. Philip Johnson and Edward M.M. Warburg (MoMA, visitors to the Bauhaus in 1927) propose inviting Josef to head the art department of the new Black Mountain College. The Alberses emigrate, arriving in New York on the S.S. Europa on November 24. S.S. Europa, arrival 1933-11-24 Consequences: The beginning of sixteen years at Black Mountain College.

Rice is abruptly dismissed in the spring of 1933; dismissals and resignations of teachers and students who side with him bring national publicity and an AAUP investigation. Investigation by the American Association of University Professors Consequences: Leads directly to the founding of Black Mountain College in 1933

Invited to come to this country, Albers replies by telegram that he does not speak English; the answer comes back: “Come anyway”. Elsewhere he describes the steps at the consulate, hopeless at first, then suddenly very quick. two telegrams Consequences: Albers leaves for BMC

At first mostly girls enroll, because the boys consider art “sissy”; interest grows to the point that even teachers join his classes. An unequaled student-teacher ratio: two to one, he exclaims. a ratio of two students per teacher mentioned
After a few English lessons, Albers goes to the village, walks into a store, and greets the clerk with “Good-bye” instead of a greeting. A classic confusion between greeting and taking leave

At the opening in 1933, everything was still to be decided: breakfast time, separate floors for men and women, the number of meals on Sunday. The debate over Sunday meals grew so heated that the supporters of three meals stopped speaking to the supporters of two. What did they mean, how many meals? Three, of course! Consequences: An illustration of the tensions of a fledgling direct democracy

Rice, unjustly dismissed from Rollins College, gathers a little under a hundred students and a handful of teachers, some of whom followed him from Rollins, in a summer hotel that stands empty nine months a year. nearly 100 students; a summer hotel unoccupied 9 months/year Consequences: The experimental college is born
In his speech, Levi describes BMC as a turbulent, brawling infant snatched in time from the womb of Rollins College fourteen years earlier. an obstetric metaphor; “fourteen years” before 1947

Ten days of hearings before the AAUP investigators, Lovejoy and Edwards: student affidavits, exchanges over the charges, the Plato-ashtray discussion, the question of loyalty. About half the teachers questioned disapprove of Rice's dismissal. 10 days of hearings; Rice receives visitors at home almost every evening, “snorts of laughter” over the latest rumors Consequences: An official report blaming Holt six months later; a preliminary report on May 25, 1933

Six months after the hearings, the report concludes that a professor who had good reason to believe his tenure secure was dismissed on charges which, even if proved, would not be upheld at most institutions; Rice is described as an exceptionally stimulating teacher who used the Socratic dialogue. Quotation: replacing received beliefs with “personal convictions reached through reflection” Consequences: Rice's official rehabilitation

After his dismissal, encouraged by his wife Nell, Rice thinks of giving up teaching and writing a play, without knowing how he would support his family. Holt had suggested that he would do better in a large institution; Lovejoy agreed: “you'd spread a little thinner”. Rice's laconic reply: “I've been in large institutions. I don't belong in institutions.”

Long discussions about creating the college; at least one lasts a whole week, with a dozen dissidents, students and teachers, at the summer house of Spurr, an old New England liberal. Aydelotte, president of Swarthmore, advises them to go ahead, but without a board of trustees, and without letting outsiders dictate policy. When someone proposes Spurr as president, he declines, since the presidency itself would contradict their principle of government by faculty and students. a renovated eighteenth-century farmhouse; Spurr, in his sixties, lives part of the year in Winter Park and had entertained Rice and Holt at his home; his son reports that he strongly disliked Rice but found his dismissal unjust Consequences: a decision to test the ideas in practice; a search for a site and for funds

Wunsch, a former drama teacher at Rollins who had gone on to teach at a high school in Louisville, suggests the buildings of the Blue Ridge Assembly near Black Mountain, North Carolina, vacant outside the summer. Georgia, who has a summer house in Highlands, is enthusiastic; he and Rice drive there. Robert E. Lee Hall, an immense building with white columns, an extraordinary view over the valley and the peaks; in Louisville, the support of his mother and sister; at Chapel Hill, his roommate was briefly Thomas Wolfe Consequences: Rice declares the site perfect: central heating, blankets, sheets, dishes for a dozen colleges

Driven by his son Frank, Rice crosses thirteen states: talking to students, coaxing parents, looking for staff. He hates begging and refuses to provide plans and charts to the Carnegie and Rockefeller foundations; he argues that above the level of masonry human behavior cannot be codified, and that a prior plan would force him to persist in a disappointing venture. The foundations politely refuse to give money without plans. two foundation secretaries so impressed that they offer to resign and come to work at Black Mountain without pay Consequences: no foundation money, but comfort in honesty

The vague ideas about the ideal organization are presented, discussed, and voted on in the first weeks — but votes are rare, since everyone agrees to keep structures and rules to a minimum, for fear that the college, like most institutions, would complete its codification at the cost of its life. Rice writes to Aydelotte that they want to keep both order and flexibility; Aydelotte replies that he has a deep prejudice against constitutions and bylaws, preferring a government of men to a government of laws, if one has the right men. Consequences: a founding principle: minimal structures

Jack Lipsey, helped by his wife Rubye and two or three helpers, cooks for the whole community. The Lipseys, who are Black, are a considerable force in the college. Each table serves itself, a volunteer fetching the dishes on a large tray and clearing afterward. breakfast served cafeteria-style; Southern cooking, vegetables cooked in fat; stacking cups and saucers as a recognized “sport” Consequences: Rubye, a college graduate, does as much counseling of the women students as anyone at the college

Jack Lipsey has firm “standards”: he refuses to serve anyone who is dirty or rude. Rice lets it be known that at breakfast, served cafeteria-style, the way Jack handed over the tray revealed his opinion of each person; several members then start picking up their own trays in the kitchen. dishes handed over in a telling way; several adopt self-service at breakfast Consequences: the cook's judgment becomes a social tool

One fine, warm fall morning, Rice asked Cramer what interested him; Cramer stammered that he wanted to understand the causes of the Depression and how to prevent future depressions; Rice laughed and told him he was placing a large order with the college. They decided that he would take Lounsbury's American history course and economics with Helen Boyden. Green rocking chairs on the porch of Lee Hall, Rice sunning himself; the Depression then at its worst; Cramer's answer: “history is sort of fun”; Rice: “You've given the college a large order!” Consequences: After Lounsbury's death, Boyden replaced the American history course with Greek history; Rice joined their discussions.

Each seminar involved four teachers present at every session, with the aim of showing how an idea looks to a group of specialists and of breaking the student of the habit of pleasing the teacher. Three seminars the first year, at 8 p.m.: “Philosophies of Social Reconstruction,” “Creative Writing,” “The Eighteenth Century”. Sessions at eight in the evening so as to have time to follow an idea; large attendance and discussions often lasting late into the night.

At each session, volunteers (teachers or students) read their writing instead of a formal assignment; there was no shortage of volunteers. One night, the argument over a story went on past midnight and resumed the next morning at breakfast.

In the college's first catalog, Rice writes that the student, made sensitive to movement, form, sound, and the other media of the arts, gains a firmer command of himself and his surroundings than through purely intellectual effort. quotation from the first catalog: “gets a firmer control of himself and his environment...” Consequences: Duberman finds these formulations derivative, vague, and romantic when they remain abstract

Rice tells everyone: “Don't ask me how or why I know it, but I know it: if I can't get the right man for art, then the thing won't work.” Some think he wants to found an art school; he thunders: “God, no! that's the last thing I want. They're the most awful places in the world!” The recommended candidates are too attached to conventional attitudes (Leonardo da Vinci invoked as the arbiter of techniques). Consequences: no candidate is suitable until the meeting at MoMA

Someone suggests that Rice talk to Edward Warburg at MoMA. Warburg and Philip Johnson (curator of architecture and industrial design) listen to him set out his plan to put art at the center of the curriculum. After a quarter of an hour of conversation, Johnson declares that he has the right man: Josef Albers, with one drawback — he does not speak a word of English. Rice replies that this is no drawback: several people at Black Mountain speak German, and interpreters will be put in his class. Johnson, according to Rice, nearly fell off his chair in astonishment. On the spot, Rice gives Johnson carte blanche to hire the Alberses immediately. a conversation of about fifteen minutes; Rice's thought: “he's blind or he's got a cleft palate” Consequences: perhaps the key decision of Black Mountain's early years, made on intuition — the way Johnson spoke of Albers, “You see a vision”

A telegram invites the Alberses to join the staff of Black Mountain in “North Carolina” — they have no idea what or where North Carolina is. An American student of Albers's in Berlin describes it as a beautiful country, very Southern and very mountainous, and encourages them to go. Albers, scrupulous, first telegraphs his admission: “I do not speak one word English.” An immediate reply: “Come anyway.” Then a long letter in German from Ted Dreier describes the school, speaking of “a pioneer adventure”: the word “pioneer,” which recalls their experience of the Bauhaus, decides them — “This is our place”. three successive telegrams; a letter in German Consequences: acceptance

Thanks to the devoted work of Edward Warburg and his committee for the rescue of German artists, the Alberses are moved ahead of a long line at the American consulate and receive non-quota visas. a long line of people waiting at the consulate Consequences: an immediate departure for the United States becomes possible
Rice, more than thirty years after taking his class, declares that Albers gave you a pair of eyes — you saw things — and that not a day goes by without his eyes saying Albers.

A teacher's wife, dominated and belittled by her husband, timidly enters Albers's class and blossoms; when the husband finds out, he forbids her to continue (“No more art”). a pencil, a sheet of paper

Albers would drop in on students between classes; once, he refused to enter Ruth Asawa's study because it was too messy and told her to send a messenger when the room was tidy. a messy study, a messenger to be sent

A student, proud of his art school background, at first judges his drawings superior to those of the amateurs; Albers tells him that he has learned only to make exact copies — he is a victim of copying, producing a photographic, lifeless line. the first weeks of the course Consequences: The student's smugness disappears

In the very first year, Loram, Sterling Professor at Yale and founder of the department of Race Relations, wants to stop at the college with his graduate students during a study tour of Black education in the South — one of them is Black. The news at once becomes a community affair: should he be treated as an ordinary guest, housed and fed with everyone, or should local mores be respected? Loram, born in South Africa, a graduate of King's College, Cambridge; Sterling Professor at Yale since 1931; the department abolished after his death in 1940; options: a Black family in the village or Jack and Rubye Lipsey's home Consequences: A community crisis

Jalowetz loses his post as head of the opera in the purge of “non-Aryan” artists; three years in Vienna, then Opernchef in Regensburg (Ratisbon), a cultural center of the Sudetenland, from 1936 to 1938; enters the United States in 1939. 1933: the purge; 1936-1938: Regensburg; 1939: entry into the United States through the National Coordinating Committee Consequences: A refugee's path to Black Mountain
Jalowetz is forced to leave his post as conductor of the Cologne Opera in the purge of “non-Aryan” artists Consequences: Three years in Vienna, then Opernchef in Regensburg

After a Village Voice article on Duberman's research, a man named Manley telephones: the Macdonald estate at Hadlyme was considered; Rice stayed there for a week with Mrs. Macdonald, of a freethinking group from Nyack. Rice's one-week stay with Mrs. Macdonald.

A group including at least one Black student (perhaps Dr. Zachariah Matthews, a South African scholar later imprisoned for his fight against apartheid) is received at the college; faced with local scandal (the very place where free love was born, it is said), the community reluctantly votes to lodge the Black student elsewhere. Peggy Bailey herself reluctantly votes for the measure; her father, used to being a voice crying in the wilderness, takes it philosophically. Not to be confused with the later visit of the anthropologist Zora Neale Hurston. letter from Mrs. George O. Barritt: all the residents of the area were scandalized; letter from Peggy Bailey to Duberman of 1970-07-26 Consequences: the community's compromise with the prevailing racism

Albers leaves Germany for the United States in 1933 and accepts a teaching post at the brand-new Black Mountain College, in western North Carolina. Consequences: The beginning of his American teaching of color.

Facing the forests of the Blue Ridge, Albers discovers with astonishment the explosion of yellows, oranges, and reds of the American fall, unlike the mostly brown foliage of northern Europe. Yellows, oranges, and reds against northern European brown. Consequences: The invention of the fall leaf studies, an American discovery.

The college is perpetually underfunded, especially during the Great Depression: the leaves, plentiful and free, are added to the students' usual colored paper. Free leaves; a college underfunded during the Depression. Consequences: Natural materials are incorporated into the color course.
During these months of crisis, he spends his monastic retreat redoing relief prints in woodcut and linocut. Woodblock and linoleum cut relief prints.

Schlemmer, who has just seen Kandinsky (who still cannot believe what has happened), reports the final closure of the Bauhaus: it is all over; an ominous silence has fallen over artistic and cultural circles; everyone is looking for a hole to hide in, a place of their own.

Looking for a head for the art department, Dreier consults his aunt; then he and Rice go up to New York to see Philip Johnson, the young head of MoMA's department of architecture and design. Johnson shows them photographs of work by Albers's students, including a sculpture made simply of wire and studies in folded paper. Rice looks up and says that this is exactly what they need. Photo of a wire sculpture; folded-paper studies. Consequences: A job offer is sent to Albers.

A first telegram reaches Berlin from Black Mountain; it is followed by a long letter in German from Ted Dreier containing the words “pioneering adventure”. Dreier writes to Albers, Johnson sends a letter, Dreier offers a thousand dollars and asks him to cable “ja” if he accepts. The money is advanced by Edward M.M. Warburg of MoMA and by Mrs. Abby Rockefeller. 1000 dollars; the expected reply: “ja”; a letter in German with “this is a pioneering adventure”. Consequences: The Alberses accept; Anni will later say that the word “pioneering” decided their choice and their long stay.
The donors who provided the start-up money in 1933 acted on faith, chose to remain anonymous for many years, and expected no return on their investment.

On the first day, the secretary, a buxom, healthy young woman, greets them on the porch, her pink, plump toes in sandals; Anni tells herself that the story of the free college must be true after all. pink, chubby toes in sandals

Josef had had only three weeks of English in Berlin before leaving; he began teaching at once, helped at first by Zastrow and Evarts as interpreters, but their translations of his idiosyncratic way of speaking turned into arguments: he dismissed them and switched to the visual, at the blackboard. three weeks of English in Berlin Consequences: visual teaching, language secondary in his class

When Albers first walks up the path to Lee Hall, a student asks him what he is going to teach; with the little English he knows, he answers: “To make open the eyes”. He will repeat variants of this sentence all his life. Consequences: It becomes the motto of his teaching: teaching art is not passing on rules, styles, or techniques, but leading to a greater awareness of what one sees and does

Albers starts the color course immediately upon his arrival. In the first year, the students mostly make color collages — the “free studies” — which they bring to class for comment. Barely able to speak English, helped first by two translators and then by Anni, he conveys his observations through gestures and pantomime. two translators at first, then Anni; collages of colored papers Consequences: Throughout the 1930s, these independent studies form an important part of the course.

Dreier, an idealist, refuses his own inheritance; most of the founding money comes from the Forbes family of Boston, friends of Dreier and Rice; the original founders are Rice, Dreier, Georgia, Lounsbury, and Feuerstein. Consequences: the creation of the college made possible

On arriving in America, Albers discovers the most brilliant fall foliage he has ever seen; since colored papers are scarce and the city (with its bookbinders) is too far away, he has leaves pressed and combines them with colored paper for his exercises. An account given by Albers himself in his lecture 4 at the University of Bridgeport, May 11, 1966 (audiotape, JAAF). Consequences: The birth of a color-course exercise combining pressed leaves and cut papers.

The faculty does without a board of trustees: it and the students in effect own the school. For lack of funds, several teachers make do with room and board. Decisions are made in the Quaker manner: each person speaks in turn until there is consensus, and elected representatives carry it out. People live and eat together, serve one another at table, and the students work in the kitchen and on the grounds to offset their costs. 22 students; room and board as the only salary Consequences: Dewey's community model: “learning by doing”

The Bauhaus, the most famous art school of the first half of the twentieth century, closes to avoid having to accept Nazi teachers; Josef Albers finds himself out of work. Consequences: Albers is available when Rice is looking for an art teacher; moreover, Anni, a former Bauhaus student and teacher, is Jewish, which makes their situation in Germany worse.

Rice, who personally knows no artists, has access to the upper reaches of MoMA; a chance but promising fifteen-minute meeting with the philanthropist Warburg and the young curator of architecture Johnson. After hearing Rice's dream of a liberal arts college placing the arts at the center of the curriculum, Johnson thinks of the right man: Josef Albers. A fifteen-minute meeting. Consequences: The recruitment of Albers, a decisive choice for the college's destiny.

Rice sends Albers a telegram inviting him to teach; Albers famously replies that he does not speak English; Rice no less famously replies that he should come anyway. Consequences: A detailed letter from Dreier in German, tickets booked, the transatlantic crossing.

Dreier, always more practical than Rice, writes the Alberses a long letter in German explaining the college, its philosophy, its status, and its limited financial resources. A long letter in German. Consequences: The Alberses accept and book their tickets.
Josef begins teaching immediately, with Anni serving as translator until his English improves.

Rice, who taught classics at Rollins, is dismissed; he founds Black Mountain College with three colleagues who left in solidarity: Lounsbury, Georgia, and Dreier. Consequences: The college is born, with no grades, no required courses, and no standardized examinations.

Albers's appointment brings into the curriculum teaching methods comparable to those of the Bauhaus and opens the influential network of the Bauhäusler to the college. Consequences: Later arrival of Anni Albers, Xanti Schawinsky, and other Bauhäusler.

When a Black student visits in the first year, the faculty debates housing him on campus; the Board of Fellows decides, without consulting the students, to find him lawful lodging in town Consequences: students draw up a petition demanding a meeting, judging the decision contrary to the institution's mission; this stopgap solution sets the policy for the following decade, the question of integration being postponed
The founding of an art school in North Carolina; the first French edition on the subject only in 2014-2015.

A creative writing manual cowritten by Wunsch and Smith, published two years before Wunsch's arrival at Black Mountain, the fruit of his experience teaching in high school and college. Eleven chapters: “Inspiration,” “Words,” “Impressions,” “Dialogue,” “Action and Conflict,” “Suggestion and Recall,” “Feeling and Mood,” “Comparison,” “Reflection and Thought,” “Imagination,” “Style” Consequences: Serves as the plan for Wunsch's first creative writing course at Black Mountain

According to Katherine Reynolds, Wunsch knew of a campus-like site 18 miles east of Asheville, just south of the town of Black Mountain, called the Blue Ridge Assembly: a group of buildings on 1,619 acres, built in 1906 by the Blue Ridge Association and used for the summer conferences and camps of the YMCA and Christian groups and for the summer program of the YMCA Graduate School. 1,619 acres, built in 1906, 18 miles east of Asheville. Consequences: The college's first campus.

Idealistic students start a first farm on the rented Blue Ridge campus, helped by local farmers and agricultural experts. Rented campus at Blue Ridge Consequences: The first of the college's two farms

Josef Albers brings his Leica from Germany when he and Anni arrive to take up their teaching posts; he offers classes and independent study in photography to interested students. Leica camera; the advent of compact cameras marketed in the mid-1920s (Leica I), making it possible to photograph in motion. Consequences: Photography is part of BMC's academic and daily life from its founding.

After the disputed dismissal of Rice and his colleagues from Rollins College, Dreier stands by Rice and cofounds Black Mountain College, where he remains a central member for the first sixteen years. Length of central presence: sixteen years Consequences: The college is born; Rice gets the public credit, Dreier secures its financial survival

Albers leaves Germany for Black Mountain College in North Carolina in 1933; he gives up glass for painting and works on paper, losing the architectural relevance of works integrated into everyday space. Consequences: A major turning point: a change of mediums and of visual teaching.
Albers arrives to teach at Black Mountain College without knowing a word of English, but manages to state his main goal: to open eyes. Consequences: The beginning of his American career.

The Bauhaus is closed more or less voluntarily by a vote of the teachers, Albers among them, under Nazi pressure (often wrongly described as a simple forced closure). Consequences: Albers and Anni (of Jewish descent) must leave Germany.

Berlin defines active support for the Bauhaus, germ cell of Bolshevism, as a political activity; Anni's Jewish heritage puts the couple in danger. The official phrase: “germ-cell of bolshevism” Consequences: The couple looks for a way out abroad.

MoMA's curator of architecture cables Albers a teaching offer on behalf of the founders of the new Black Mountain College. A telegram, an offer quickly accepted Consequences: The couple arrives in America, where they will stay for the rest of their lives.

Albers immediately sets up classes for beginners; the general schedule is organized around these classes; the drawing class stays full of students, teachers, and members of the community. A contemporary visitor judges Albers's classes “the largest and, with Rice's, the most dramatic”

Lacking the facilities and resources for sandblasting glass, Albers produces no more works in glass after Germany; he prefers the stability of a permanent post and a guaranteed income, however meager. Exception: Rolled Wrongly (1931), refabricated in New York after 1956 Consequences: A profound turning point in his art: gouaches, prints, then oil paintings.

Union Carbide presents a three-room house made entirely of Vinylite: modular walls with a double layer of Vinylite-lacquered aluminum around an insulating layer, doors of Vinylite panels on particleboard, floor tiles so durable that they were reinstalled at Union Carbide's headquarters. The floor tiles stayed there for more than twenty-five years Consequences: Shows the utopian dreams attached to plastic, similar to those attached to glass in Germany
Lounsbury, a lawyer who came from Rollins, dies shortly after the college opens.

At the end of the first term, the faculty numbers eleven and there are twenty-two students. 11 teachers, 22 students; four from Rollins: Rice, Dreier (mathematics), Georgia (chemistry), Lounsbury (law).

In their search for an art teacher, Rice and Dreier are led to MoMA, where the architect Philip Johnson recommends Josef Albers, who taught the preliminary course at the Bauhaus. Consequences: Albers warns that he does not speak English; the college replies that it cannot guarantee that it will exist for more than a year.

At the welcoming ceremony on his arrival in 1933, Albers replies: “I want to open eyes,” a phrase signaling his commitment as a teacher and his wish to train an audience in new perceptual strategies. Consequences: The founding formula of Albers's teaching at the college

A dispute over faculty governance breaks out at Rollins College; the ousted supporters, including the first rector, John Andrew Rice, come before an AAUP mediation panel, which upholds their actions but cannot reinstate them. AAUP mediation; a favorable verdict but no reinstatement. Consequences: A decision to found an institution that avoids the pitfalls of an autocratic chancellor.

Early in 1933, the Gestapo forces the closure of the Bauhaus; the Alberses find themselves without work or a future, their art being out of favor with the new government; Anni, of Jewish origin, senses the dangers. Josef is 45, Anni 33 in November 1933 Consequences: Emigration to the United States
Goodman writes and dates “A Cross-Country Runner at Sixty-Five” in New York City, 1933, before Black Mountain College existed. handwritten note “New York City 1933” at the end of the text

In 1933 the Gestapo padlocks the doors of the Bauhaus; three months later Mies van der Rohe, its last director, obtains the right to reopen the school but chooses to close it for good. Three months between the Gestapo closure and the dissolution. Consequences: Opens the way for the Alberses' emigration to America.

Shortly after the closure of the Bauhaus, the architect Philip Johnson, an admirer of Anni Albers's textile work, asks the couple whether they would like to go to America; they accept. In New York, Johnson learns that a new college is being founded at Black Mountain (North Carolina), with art at the center of the curriculum, whose founders are looking for a great art teacher; he suggests Josef Albers. Anni and Josef warn that he does not speak English; Johnson replies that they should come anyway. Consequences: Albers is hired at Black Mountain College.
